name: Adult-onset Still disease
aliases: systemic-onset juvenile idiopathic arthritis in adults

reference.source: Firestein & Kelley's Textbook of Rheumatology / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Classic triad of high spiking quotidian fevers, an evanescent salmon-pink rash appearing with fever spikes, and arthralgia or arthritis
Markedly elevated serum ferritin, often with a low glycosylated ferritin fraction, supports the diagnosis
It is a diagnosis of exclusion (e.g. Yamaguchi criteria) requiring the ruling out of infection, malignancy, and other autoimmune disease
Sore throat, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and serositis are common accompanying features
Rheumatoid factor and antinuclear antibody are characteristically negative, and there is a neutrophilic leucocytosis
Macrophage activation syndrome (secondary haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis) is a life-threatening complication to watch for
Treatment ranges from NSAIDs and systemic corticosteroids to IL-1 and IL-6 blockade in refractory or systemic disease
reference.pathophysiology: Adult-onset Still disease is a systemic autoinflammatory disorder driven by dysregulation of the innate immune system rather than autoantibody-mediated autoimmunity. Activation of macrophages and neutrophils with overproduction of proinflammatory cytokines, particularly interleukin-1, interleukin-6, interleukin-18, and tumour necrosis factor, produces the fever, rash, arthritis, and hyperferritinaemia. Interleukin-18 and macrophage activation underlie the extreme ferritin elevation and the propensity to macrophage activation syndrome. A genetic predisposition combined with an infectious or other environmental trigger is thought to initiate the process.
additionalDifferentials: Sepsis and other systemic infections (including viral)
Systemic lupus erythematosus and other connective tissue diseases
Reactive arthritis and other seronegative arthropathies
Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS)
additionalInvestigations: Serum ferritin, characteristically very high, with glycosylated ferritin fraction if available
Full blood count showing neutrophilic leucocytosis and inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP)
Blood cultures and infective screen to exclude sepsis
Autoantibody panel (rheumatoid factor and antinuclear antibody typically negative)
Imaging and lymph node biopsy where malignancy or lymphoma needs exclusion
Liver function tests, triglycerides, and fibrinogen to detect emerging macrophage activation syndrome
redFlags: Features of macrophage activation syndrome: falling cell counts, very high ferritin, hypertriglyceridaemia, and organ dysfunction
Rapidly progressive hepatic dysfunction or coagulopathy
Persistent constitutional decline raising concern for occult malignancy
reference.prognosis: The course is variable: some have a self-limiting monocyclic illness, others a polycyclic relapsing course, and a subset develop chronic destructive arthritis; macrophage activation syndrome is the principal cause of mortality.
pitfalls: Diagnosing it before adequately excluding infection and malignancy
Missing evolving macrophage activation syndrome when cytopenias develop
Dismissing the diagnosis because the transient rash is absent at the time of review
Over-reliance on ferritin alone, which is nonspecific
Failing to escalate to cytokine-directed therapy in corticosteroid-refractory disease
management: Control systemic inflammation with corticosteroids as first-line therapy for significant disease, tapering as fever, rash and arthritis settle
Use non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for mild fever and arthralgia while confirming the diagnosis
Add a steroid-sparing agent such as methotrexate for persistent arthritis or steroid dependence
Escalate refractory or systemic disease to biologic therapy targeting interleukin-1 (anakinra, canakinumab) or interleukin-6 (tocilizumab)
Treat macrophage activation syndrome urgently with high-dose corticosteroids and interleukin-1 blockade, escalating to intensive care support
Monitor ferritin, blood counts, liver function, triglycerides and fibrinogen to detect emerging macrophage activation syndrome
Continue to exclude infection and malignancy before and during immunosuppression, given diagnosis is by exclusion
Refer to rheumatology with physiotherapy and orthopaedic input for chronic destructive arthritis
